newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: North-South clash seen likely at world trade meet.
newsitem.headline: North-South clash seen likely at world trade meet.

text.p: Ambassadors to the World Trade Organisation were on Thursday reported far from agreeing a key policy text, making almost certain that a ministerial meeting in Singapore next month would see North-South confrontation.

Three weeks after a declaration by the ministers setting the trade agenda to the end of the century was due to have been completed, four days and nights of sometimes heated debate had failed to produce a final version, diplomats said.

"There is little hope now it can be done in time for Singapore," said one envoy after a late night session on Wednesday was suspended after what he said had been some tense moments pitting developed against some developing countries.

"It is a pity, but I can't see that we can avoid passing on the problems on to the ministers, and that will mean a confrontation there too," said another source close to the negotiations, due to resume later on Thursday.

Trade ministers from the 125 current members of the WTO, as well as from many of the 30 other countries waiting to come in, are gathering in the Asian city-state from December 8-13 for the two-year-old body's first Ministerial Meeting.

The declaration was intended to be a signal of their commitment to push ahead with opening world trade in goods, services, textiles and farm produce and extending the process of globalisation of the international economy.

WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero said on Wednesday the ministers should use the gathering "to deliver a political message of confidence and support" for the global trading system of agreed rules that his organisation supervises.

But debate on its content, started several months ago, has brought out simmering differences between the big powers -- the United States, the European Union, Japan and Canada -- and key emerging economies like India, Malaysia and even Argentina.

The problems range from whether controversial new issues like labour, investment and competition policy should come onto the WTO agenda, to the speed of opening of textile markets and how soon new talks on freer agrcultural trade should be started.
Ruggiero, in a bid to find compromises, presented a draft text last week -- and opened the way for several days, and long nights, of argument since.

The latest setback, trade sources and diplomats said, was a sudden request from Argentina -- a member of the 13-member Cairns Group of farm-exporting countries -- on Wednesday evening for a separate clause to be included on agriculture.

Agreements on freeing agricultural trade, the first to be covered by a multilateral accord, were reached in the 1986-93 Uruguay Round of world trade negotiations, and new talks on extending them are due to begin by the year 2000.
Latin American members of the Cairns Group, which also includes Australia and New Zealand, have already made clear they want preparations to begin well in advance.

But they met strong resistance from the EU as well as Japan and South Korea who were already forced to open up their long tight-shut rice markets at the end of the Round and are keen to postpone pressure for further liberalisation.

On the "new issues", Asian developing countries -- who see them as part of an offensive by the big powers to allow Western- and Japanese-based multinationals to seize control of their economies -- are standing firm on saying "no."

They are also accusing the industrialised powers, especially the United States and the EU, of violating the spirit of the Round accords on textiles by maintaining tight controls on clothing imports from the South.
